title: Setting the bar
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien argues that schools proclaim high expectations for students but rarely hold them in practice, and rarely set them for staff at all. On the student side he points to lenient promotion policies, 40 to 50 percent pass marks that students clear with surprising precision, and a non-scored pathway used to trim a school's results tail. On the staff side he criticizes box-ticking development plans, meetings used to deliver information that belongs in an email, checklist-style observation that caps teacher expertise, and weak engagement with research. His conclusion is that high expectations are not micromanagement but the condition for improvement, and that culture spirals downward when they slip.
points: Schools talk about high expectations while structural policies on promotion, pass marks and non-scored pathways quietly lower the bar for students.
Pass marks set low produce results that cluster just above the line, since if you set the bar to the floor people will find a way under it.
Staff expectations are equally lax: perfunctory development plans let teachers repeat the same curriculum regardless of outcomes.
Meetings that only deliver information tell staff that emails need not be read and that their expertise is not valued.
Leaders should teach principles (why) rather than checklists of strategies, and observe effectiveness rather than presence of boxes.
quotes: This sends a pretty powerful message that high expectations do not matter because regardless of their results they will be moving on up to the next year level with their friends.
I’ve long said that if you set the bar to the floor, not only will people still not clear it, they will bring a shovel and find a way under it.
I am strongly of the belief that any meeting should create something that is instantly actionable for a staff member.
This sends a blaringly loud message to staff that they do not need to read their emails but also that their knowledge and expertise is not valued.
When practice becomes too prescriptive it can be constraining to the expertise of the teacher in the room.
By not engaging with research at an individual and school level we are telling staff that whatever they have always done is good enough.
Unless we set the bar high we will never know what people are truly capable of.
